prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: I still put B023 first, but I have changed the configuration. The third name is now Dorn and not Katz. The claim of the work is that shocks to labour demand, from technology and from trade, reach workers and places through adjustment that is slow and costly, and that this can be measured credibly. The China-shock papers (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) show this for trade. The Autor-Dorn work on job polarisation and local labour markets shows it for technology. So the trio covers both strands with the same core authors, the same local-labour-market designs and the same data. That answers Krusell's request that a B023 prize stay within one strand, and the chair's question whether technology and trade shocks are one achievement. I now think they are, provided the citation is about empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment and does not claim the task-model theory. That theory sits partly with Acemoglu and Restrepo, outside the credited names and inside the 2024 prize. The work is mature, with a technology strand of decades and a trade strand of more than a decade. The core findings of persistent local effects and costly reallocation have survived replication, criticism of shift-share inference and debate over magnitudes. It affects labour, trade, macro and public policy, including today's automation debate. I apply the same standard to B006 and B036. I cannot judge from field proximity, and my own work on growth and structural change is not labour demand in this sense.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is unchanged: B023 combines two related strands, and any three names leave out someone with a real claim. Katz is now excluded, even though his wage-structure and skill-biased change evidence is the foundation of the technology strand, and that omission is a real cost. The overlap with the 2021 (Card), 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes must count under the same standard that members apply to B006's proximity to 2022. I think the Dorn trio reduces that overlap but does not remove it. The size and persistence of the trade-shock effects and the shift-share identification are still debated. I also accept that a Kiyotaki-Moore pair (B006) now has the cleanest attribution on the list. If the committee decides that B023 still merges two discoveries, B006 is my fallback. A B006 prize with a mechanism that organised a large research programme and passed the 2008 test would be a defensible outcome in my view.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B023 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that the Autor-Dorn-Hanson papers are the unified, jointly authored core, that Katz's skill-premium work overlaps with the Goldin-Katz tradition recognised in 2023, and that the citation should rest on empirical evidence about labour-demand shocks and not on task-model theory, which partly sits with Acemoglu and Restrepo.
responses.response: You moved me. In round 1 I kept Katz because he anchors the technology side. But the same-design, same-data core is Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and Autor and Dorn also have a polarisation and local-labour-market paper on the technology side, so the trio does not give up that strand. This is also the better answer to the Goldin overlap, which I should have weighed more heavily. I agree on wording the citation around empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment. I recall the authorship from background knowledge and have not verified it. I would still say openly that Katz's earlier wage-structure work is excluded and is a real cost.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B047 first and B023 third. He would give only Autor and Hanson on B023 for the tightest attribution. He argues that the China-shock papers belong to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, that the task and skill-bias work involves Katz and others, and that a bundle which omits Dorn is harder to defend than a single method with a clear core.
responses.response: I agree with half of this. The bundling concern is mine too, and it is why Katz is no longer in my trio. I disagree with the two-name cut. Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers and the polarisation work, so dropping him to keep the number small would omit an originator for the sake of neatness. Your point that BLP's core credit is easier to trace to specific papers is fair. My claim is only that Autor, Dorn and Hanson now have a comparable paper trail for a labour-demand citation. We differ on how much weight tight attribution should get against breadth of influence across fields. I do not think either of us has shown that one criterion decides it.

responses.point: Hassler's round-1 file prefers B006 with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler, with the citation tied to collateral constraints and balance-sheet frictions and not to the accelerator or the bank-run themes of the 2022 prize. He ranks B023 below B006 because its credit is spread across the tasks, trade and Katz, Dorn and Acemoglu boundaries.
responses.response: In round 1 I answered a two-name proposal, and I should anchor on your file instead, which is three-name. Your ask that the citation explicitly exclude the accelerator and deposit-insurance themes is the right standard, and I would apply the same standard to B023 by excluding the task-model theory. Your boundary objection to B023 has moved me, since I have dropped Katz and narrowed the citation. Whether a prize resting on Gertler's later intermediary work is separable from Bernanke is the open question. I cannot settle it, and it is why a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is the safer B006 configuration. I still rank B023 first on the breadth of the evidence base. The B006 channel's direct empirical identification is mixed, as you acknowledge. That is a judgement of weight, not a claim that B006 is weak.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B006 first and B023 third. He says B023 joins two strands with partly different originators, that its credit overlaps with Goldin-Katz and Acemoglu, and that if the committee prefers B023 it should favour a version that stays within one of the two strands. He says a mechanism need not be settled in every empirical detail to be prize-worthy, provided it organised a large research programme and survived 2008.
responses.response: I take both points. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson version is my attempt at your single-strand request. It centres on empirical evidence about labour-demand shocks and local adjustment, not on a bundle of wage-structure theory. On your general standard I agree that a mechanism does not need every channel pinned down. The difference is that B023 offers designs that have been re-examined and refined for a decade or more, and I weigh that heavily. I accept the 2008 vindication of B006 as a serious counterweight. I do not treat the number of members who rank B006 first as evidence of merit, and I recognise that you and I are frequent co-authors, so I flag that I am not relying on that familiarity.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B047 first and B036 as an alternative. She says Stromberg and Hassler persuaded her that Melitz built on contemporaneous firm-level work (Bernard-Jensen, Eaton-Kortum) outside the credited names, so B036's credit boundary is less clear than BLP's. She earlier favoured Autor-Dorn-Hanson over Katz for B023.
responses.response: I agree on B036, and it is why I replaced it among my alternatives. I had ranked it fifth, and the credit-boundary problem you describe, with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Yeaple outside the credited names, is a larger defect than I weighed in round 1. I replaced it with B003, whose Mian-Sufi pair is clean. I take your preference for the Dorn variant of B023 as support for my change, though I note that you also see the Katz overlap with Goldin as a real concern, and that I cannot claim to have settled it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats technology and trade shocks as one coherent achievement when the citation is limited to empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment, or still as two strands.

Whether Katz's omission is acceptable. His wage-structure evidence anchors the technology strand, and I now judge his overlap with Goldin and the wider Acemoglu boundary to weigh against him, but the choice with Dorn remains close.
How much of Autor and Dorn's technology-side contribution is distinct from work already recognised in 2023 and 2024, and whether the empirical wording of the citation is enough to separate it.
How persistent and how large the local labour-market effects are, and how robust shift-share inference is. I rely on background recall, not verified citation or replication data.

Whether a Kiyotaki-Moore pair (B006) is separable enough from the 2022 prize to outrank B023 on common criteria. I cannot settle this myself, and I would regard it as a defensible alternative outcome.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile: I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and have co-authored with John Hassler, both fellow committee members and IIES colleagues. Both have given round-1 views on these candidates, and I disclose this without adjudicating it. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, credited on B034, which is not in my preferred configuration or alternatives. My research uses heterogeneous-agent macro methods related to B043, which is also not in my configuration. None of Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz appears among my listed co-authors, and no such tie to my alternatives B006 or B003 is apparent from the supplied profile. As a committee member I have co-authored popular summaries of earlier prizes. I do not claim any private knowledge of the proceedings.
